entry.evidence: However, the relationships were not researched in-depth in the context of Sri Lanka

steps.action: Pose the gap: the seasonal variation of six pollutants in Sri Lankan cities and their relation to meteorology is not well studied with long continuous records.
steps.quote: Moreover, the relationship between air pollutant and meteorological variables is not well studied with the recently updated data sets.

steps.action: Use hourly PM2.5, PM10, NO2, SO2, CO and O3 records from commercial analysers, plus hourly meteorological records, at two Central Environmental Authority stations (Battaramulla/Colombo and Kandy) over 30 months.
steps.quote: collected in hourly intervals from January 2019 to May 2021 (for 30 months)

steps.action: Group the record into the four naturally recurring monsoon and intermonsoon seasons (NEM, FIM, SWM, SIM) defined by wind direction.
steps.quote: adopted the aforementioned monthly groups to identify the seasonal distribution of air pollutant concentration

steps.action: Choose the analyses: Pearson correlation matrices in R (corrplot) and bivariate polar plots of concentration by wind speed and direction (openair).
steps.quote: the pollutant concentrations and wind speed with directions were plotted in the polar plots

steps.action: Describe seasonal diurnal cycles at both stations: bimodal morning and evening peaks for PM, CO and NO2, a midday single peak for O3 in Colombo, and flat SO2 in Kandy (Figure 2).
steps.quote: follow a similar bimodal distribution pattern

steps.action: Attribute the peaks post hoc to rush-hour traffic, and also to mixing height, turbulence and wind, without separating these causes.
steps.quote: peaks of pollutants are ascribed to the variations of mixing height, vertical turbulence, and horizontal wind velocity and emission characteristics

steps.action: Describe monthly daytime box plots: Colombo highest December to March and lowest July to September; Kandy follows a different timing (Figure 3).
steps.quote: the highest average concentrations of trace pollutant gases and particulate matter are observed from December to March

steps.action: Explain the higher SO2 in Battaramulla by wind transport from power plants and industries and by heavier vehicle traffic in Colombo.
steps.quote: polluted air from power plants and industries can be transported to Battaramulla AQMS by the wind

steps.action: Describe monthly nighttime box plots and contrast them with daytime at each station (Figure 4).
steps.quote: the monthly variation of the mean concentrations of mentioned pollutants follows a similar pattern to that of daytime

steps.action: Tabulate seasonal day and night means (Table 1): Colombo maxima in NEM and minima in SWM; Kandy maxima in FIM and SWM.
steps.quote: concentrations of pollutants in the Battaramulla are recorded for the NEM season compared to other seasons

steps.action: Compare the Colombo seasonal pattern with Grange et al. (winter postmonsoon maxima, monsoon minima) and report agreement.
steps.quote: consistent with that of Grange et al. [39]

steps.action: Adopt literature explanations for the seasonal contrast (boundary-layer dilution, wind ventilation) and for day/night differences (stagnant night air, daytime photochemistry).
steps.quote: due to the dilution of surface emissions into a deeper atmospheric boundary layer

steps.action: Propose that Kandy's complex terrain (valley sheltering, stable layers, mountain-valley breezes) explains higher daytime concentrations despite fewer nearby industries.
steps.quote: which favors pollutant accumulation at the lowest levels

steps.action: Compute season-by-season Pearson correlations (5% significance) between each pollutant and temperature, humidity, solar radiation, rainfall, wind speed and wind direction at both stations (Figures 5 and 6).
steps.quote: determined by using Pearson correlation analysis

steps.action: Set the correlation signs for O3, CO, PM, NO2, SO2, rainfall and NO2–O3 against cited studies: mostly agreement, but contrary to Yoo et al. on rainfall.
steps.quote: Similarly, other researchers [51–53] observed

steps.action: Examine the dependence of each pollutant on wind speed and direction with polar plots for one season per station (SWM Colombo, NEM Kandy), reading source directions off the plots (Figures 7 and 8).
steps.quote: polar plots were used to investigate the dependence of pollutants on wind speed and wind direction

steps.action: Match the rush-hour double peaks and the daytime O3/NOx inverse relation to reports from Chennai, Kathmandu, Sao Paulo and Indian sites.
steps.quote: two peaks of pollutants corresponding to the morning and evening rush

steps.action: Explain the Colombo seasonality by monsoon wind paths: SWM air from the Arabian Sea crosses few sources; NEM air crosses power plants and industrial estates.
steps.quote: low-level jets from the Arabian sea direction toward the air quality monitoring station cross fewer pollutant sources

steps.action: Keep the claim that wind speed and direction are the key meteorological drivers of the seasonal variation in both cities.
steps.quote: wind speed and direction is the key meteorological component for observed seasonal variation of pollutant concentrations in two cities

steps.action: Raise open questions for future work: sea-breeze influence and back-trajectory analysis by season.
steps.quote: it is highly recommended to conduct the trajectory analysis

steps.action: Conclude that meteorology and emissions drive the diurnal and seasonal cycles, and that annual PM means lie below the national guideline values.
steps.quote: the annual average concentration of PM2.5 and PM10 in the two cities was less than the air quality guideline values

tree.answer: Diurnal and seasonal variation of six pollutants at two Sri Lankan urban stations
Yes; concentrations measured hourly at fixed stations
Characterize seasonality and its association with meteorological variables
Mechanisms named post hoc (traffic, mixing height, monsoon wind transport, terrain), not set up as testable rivals
No distinct predictions derived for any rival
Conditions found: naturally recurring monsoon seasons

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes; seasons recur across about 2.5 annual cycles
Not tested; no robustness or independent-data checks performed
Seasonal regularity and wind dependence retained

end.claim: At Colombo and Kandy in 2019–2021, all pollutants vary significantly by season (Colombo highest in the northeast monsoon, a contrasting pattern in Kandy), with wind speed and direction the most influential meteorological factor except for SO2 and O3.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the 30-month hourly co-located pollutant and meteorological records from the two monitoring stations, neither the seasonal patterns nor the correlations would exist.

gates.evidence: The data came from monitoring stations set up under a vehicular emission testing programme, not chosen by a hypothesis (p. 2). The correlations were screened at a 5% significance level (p. 11), so individual correlations could have failed. Seasonal differences were called significant without a reported test, and the causal attributions (traffic, wind transport, terrain) were never put to a test. Nothing was fixed before the data except the conventional season definitions and the 5% level.

imports.item: Pearson correlation coefficient with significance screening
R software with the corrplot package
Chemiluminescence, UV fluorescence, NDIR and UV absorption gas analysers; beta-attenuation particulate monitor

novelty_claims.quote: has not been previously reported for urban cities in Sri Lanka
very few studies have worked on the seasonal variation of pollutants in Sri Lanka

limits: No V check is performed here. The Kandy station is a second site in the design, not a deliberate replication. There is no sensitivity analysis, no alternative season grouping, no detrending, and no handling of autocorrelation in the correlations. Sub-claims: the attributions of the peaks to traffic, of Colombo seasonality to monsoon wind paths, and of Kandy levels to terrain are best_explanation at most; they are asserted, not tested (inference). Polar plots cover only one season per station. The introduction promises a COVID-19 lockdown analysis that is not carried out. There are internal inconsistencies: the abstract gives 3 years 2018–2021 while the methods give 30 months 2019–2021; the text gives Kandy FIM PM10 as 41.2 while Table 1 gives 51.1; the text says 'SWM season of 2013'. The process behind analysis choices is not documented (inference). The data are not public. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence was coded.

disagreements.target: Previous studies [59] (Yoo et al.) reporting significant negative pollutant–rainfall correlations from precipitation scavenging
disagreements.support: No pollutant was significantly correlated with rainfall in any season at either station; the paper cites Beijing results [58] as agreeing.

disagreements.target: Established negative NO2–O3 correlation (Miyama et al. [56])
disagreements.support: The negative relation holds in Battaramulla in all seasons but weakens in Kandy (Figure 6).
disagreements.quote: However, the relationship is getting weak in Kandy, as shown in Figure 6.

disagreements.target: Sly et al. [33] on indoor pollution being the greater threat in South and Southeast Asia
disagreements.support: The authors argue that Sri Lanka-specific data are insufficient to support the conclusion; they offer no new evidence.
disagreements.quote: to conclude that indoor air pollution is more harmful to respiratory health than outdoor pollutants levels

alternatives_considered.chosen: Orographic sheltering, stable layers and mountain-valley circulation favoring pollutant accumulation in Kandy
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Local industrial emissions (implicitly set aside because fewer industries are near the Kandy station)
alternatives_considered.reason: Fewer industries are located near Kandy AQMS, yet daytime concentrations are higher than in Battaramulla
